parts: Lesson 29: Optional Module B: Photojournalism — Summary

With the coming of photography news could be conveyed with greater authority and emphasis; photographs started supporting the written news in newspapers and magazines and photojournalism was born. Early war photographers were the first war photojournalists. Around the 1880s a technology called half tone made it possible to print photographs in newspapers. Photojournalism today is news photography: photographs that support the story of a news event, taken by photojournalists, who often can also write a few words in support of the photograph.

Sports photojournalism (specialised skill and equipment, e.g. cricket); war photojournalism (the earliest form; photographers risking their lives in conflicts and riots); glamour photojournalism (film stars and famous people; such photographers are called paparazzi, an Italian word); spot news photojournalism (day-to-day news such as political events, crime and accidents; the most common and most demanding); travel photojournalism (documentation of an area's landscape, people, cultures, customs and history; amateurs share photographs online through photo-sharing websites); wildlife photojournalism (one of the more challenging forms, needs advanced equipment and knowledge of animal behaviour and terrain). Photojournalists may be employed by a newspaper or freelancers who sell pictures to newspapers and agencies. Scope extends to web-based photojournalism; newspapers and websites also use photos sent by ordinary people with mobile cameras.

A photograph must speak for itself ('a single picture is worth a thousand words'). Composition is the placement of the subject or subjects within the picture frame; it creates impact (a beggar near the camera and a rich man in a big car in the distance shows contrast), makes the picture appealing and energetic (action photographs of war or sports) and demands balance. The rule of thirds is the most common basic rule of framing: elements should fall roughly on the intersections of the lines dividing the frame into three rows and three columns. Camera angle affects composition: a camera below the person's eye level makes the person appear larger (used for leaders and film personalities) and a top angle (above eye level) makes the person look smaller.

A photo feature (photo essay) is a story or essay on a subject told using photographs (a family told in five pictures: meal, father leaving for work, mother cooking, daughter back from school, grandparents watching TV). It is generally conceived at the editor's desk, who briefs the photo editor. A photo editor is the overall in charge of the photo section of a newspaper or magazine; he chooses the photographer, discusses the topic, may choose a reporter to write around the essay, and selects the best pictures that convey the whole story.
